questions.question: Which statement best explains most cases of hyponatremia?
choices: The sodium concentration is low relative to body water
The body has no sodium remaining
Every case results from drinking too little water
The finding always proves extracellular volume excess
questions.explanation: Hyponatremia is primarily a water-to-sodium concentration disorder. Total-body sodium and extracellular volume may be low, near normal, or increased, so volume assessment and tonicity are required.

questions.question: Why can acute hypotonic hyponatremia cause neurologic deterioration?
choices: Water moves out of brain cells and shrinks them
Water moves into brain cells and promotes cerebral edema
Sodium directly blocks every neuron
Plasma proteins immediately leave the circulation
questions.explanation: A hypotonic extracellular environment drives water into cells. Brain swelling can cause headache, confusion, seizures, reduced consciousness, respiratory compromise, and herniation.

questions.question: A client has hyponatremia, ascites, dependent edema, and heart failure. Which volume pattern is most consistent with these findings?
choices: Hypovolemic hyponatremia with no retained fluid
Hypervolemic hyponatremia in which water gain exceeds sodium gain
Hypernatremia caused by free-water loss
Pseudohyponatremia proven by edema alone
questions.explanation: Heart failure can produce sodium and water retention with proportionally greater water retention, resulting in edema and dilutional hyponatremia. Effective circulating volume may still be reduced.

questions.question: A low sodium result occurs with marked hyperglycemia. What is the safest interpretation?
choices: It automatically confirms hypotonic hyponatremia
Glucose and measured osmolality must be considered because water may have shifted into extracellular fluid
The sodium result can be ignored without assessment
The client must have SIADH
questions.explanation: Marked hyperglycemia can create hypertonicity and shift water out of cells, lowering measured sodium. The mechanism differs from routine hypotonic hyponatremia and requires contextual interpretation.

questions.question: Which client with hyponatremia requires the highest priority response?
choices: Client with a stable mild value and no symptoms
Client with a new seizure and decreasing level of consciousness
Client asking why urine testing was ordered
Client whose repeat specimen is pending and remains at baseline
questions.explanation: Seizure and declining consciousness suggest severe hyponatremic encephalopathy. ABC assessment, emergency assistance, seizure precautions, and protocol-based treatment are immediate priorities.

questions.question: Hypertonic saline is prescribed for severe symptomatic hyponatremia. Which nursing action is essential?
choices: Increase the rate independently if symptoms persist
Verify the concentration, pump settings, monitoring schedule, and prescribed correction limits
Stop neurologic checks once the infusion begins
Encourage unlimited water intake during the infusion
questions.explanation: Hypertonic saline is high-alert therapy. Controlled administration, serial sodium testing, neurologic reassessment, and prompt response to an unexpectedly rapid rise reduce treatment-related harm.

questions.question: Why is overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia dangerous?
choices: Adapted brain cells may lose water rapidly, risking osmotic demyelination
It always causes immediate pulmonary embolism
It permanently prevents renal filtration
It converts sodium into potassium
questions.explanation: During chronic hyponatremia, brain cells shed osmoles to limit swelling. Rapid correction can then pull water from adapted cells and contribute to osmotic demyelination, which may present after a delay.

questions.question: Which finding most strongly suggests impaired ADH effect in a client with hypernatremia?
choices: Very high urine output with persistently dilute urine
Small amount of concentrated urine after poor intake
Dependent edema with oliguria
Dark stool after iron therapy
questions.explanation: When ADH is deficient or the kidney cannot respond, free water is lost in a large volume of dilute urine. Hypernatremia develops if intake cannot match the loss.

questions.question: A client with hypernatremia is hypotensive, confused, and poorly perfused. Which plan reflects the correct priority?
choices: Correct the sodium concentration without considering circulation
Support ABCs and prescribed intravascular resuscitation first, then address free-water deficit with serial monitoring
Delay all treatment until thirst returns
Give unlimited oral water despite reduced consciousness
questions.explanation: Shock threatens organ perfusion immediately and may require prescribed isotonic resuscitation before slower free-water correction. Reduced consciousness also makes unassessed oral intake unsafe.

questions.question: Which finding during correction of a sodium disorder requires immediate escalation?
choices: Sodium is changing within the prescribed target and mentation is improving
New seizure with a sodium change faster than the prescribed limit
Urine output is being measured accurately
The client can explain the monitoring plan
questions.explanation: A new seizure and unexpectedly rapid sodium change may signal dangerous osmotic brain injury or ongoing severe disease. Stop, assess ABCs, obtain emergency help, and follow the prescribed escalation pathway.
